name: al-Tabari
label: Outside witness
otherNames: Abu Djafar Mohammed ibn Djarir at-Tabari, the form on the title page of the Leiden edition
Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir, as a later summary printed in that edition names him in Arabic
Abu Ga'far al Tabari, in the Latin translation of the chronicle of Elias of Nisibis
knownFor: A Muslim chronicler of Baghdad whose year-by-year annals tell how the Muslim armies met Christians, among them the priests and monks of Hira and the Christians of Merv who buried the last Persian king.
dates: Born in the year 224 of the hijra and died in 310, by F. K. Ginzel (1887), who names no source. Philip Hitti (1916) also gives his death in 310. Neither gives the years in the Christian calendar
place: Baghdad, where Ginzel calls him a chronicler and Hitti says he died. Hitti, from al-Fihrist and Ibn Khallikan, says he traveled in Egypt, Syria and Iraq to study. No source gives his birthplace

keyWorks.title: Annals (Annales, in the Latin of the Leiden edition)
keyWorks.about: a history arranged year by year. Philip Hitti calls it the first complete series of annals. The Library holds the Arabic only for the years from late 11 to 32 of the hijra, in two volumes of the Leiden edition (1890 and 1893), each with a Latin summary of contents

keyWorks.title: Commentary on the Quran (Tafsir)
keyWorks.about: which Axel Moberg, in 1924, calls his great commentary on the Koran. Moberg says most Muslim interpreters refer the Quran's verses on the pit to the Najran martyrs. He says the commentary also gives traditions that refer them to an incident among the Parsees, or to "Daniel and his men". Not held

keyWorks.title: A short work on the witnesses of traditions
keyWorks.about: which the Leiden edition planned as an appendix (opusculum de testibus traditionum). Not held

traces: The Christian chronicler Elias of Nisibis names al-Tabari's Annals among his Arabic sources, his editors say. Elias cites him in most years from 275 to 302 of the hijra.

The book of the churches and monasteries of Egypt that B. T. A. Evetts edited in 1895, under the name of Abu Salih the Armenian, cites "the testimony of the history of At-Tabari". Evetts says its author had studied "The great history of At-Tabari".

The historian al-Maqrizi died in 1441, Evetts says. Étienne Quatremère's French of 1811 quotes al-Maqrizi on the caliph Aziz's library. Aziz had more than twenty copies of al-Tabari's history, one written in the author's own hand.
Hitti says the lost histories of al-Mada'ini are known only by excerpts through al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari and Yakut.
remembered: Hitti calls him "The most illustrious writer on history after al-Baladhuri". He says al-Tabari's method of writing year by year was followed by Ibn al-Athir and Abu l-Fida, and won more favor than the system of al-Mas'udi.
Ginzel says he is counted the most reliable of the Muslim annalists, and that he mostly recorded what he lived through or had on good authority.

uncertain: He writes as a Muslim, two centuries after the conquests he describes, and passes on reports as they reached him, often in more than one version. His life rests on two short modern notes. Hitti draws on al-Fihrist and Ibn Khallikan, and Ginzel names no source.

How far to trust him. Ginzel says he is counted the most reliable of the Muslim annalists, for what he lived through or had on good authority. Ginzel tested one of al-Tabari's eclipse reports, which al-Tabari gives as something said, for the year 281. On that date there was only a slight eclipse, not visible at the town named. One in 280, the year Elias of Nisibis gives, fits fully. Hitti says Arab historians did little to analyze, compare or test their reports. Their rule, in his words, was "what has been once well said need not be told again", and al-Tabari's preface voices it.

His sources for the conquests. The Hira report of 190,000 and the Najran report reach him through a chain of tellers, al-Sari from Shu'ayb from Sayf ibn Umar. The Hira report of 90,000 comes by another chain, through Salama. The name after Salama is unreadable in the scan, but elsewhere in the volume Salama's chain reaches Ibn Ishaq, the biographer of Muhammad. A later summary printed in the Leiden edition says he had the Jerusalem story from Sayf too.

Versions side by side. He gives three accounts of how Christians at Merv buried Yazdegerd. In one, the bishop of Merv takes the body from the river. In another, the body catches on a branch, and the bishop takes it and lays it in a vault where he used to sit. On the same page, E. Prym, who edited this volume of the Annals in 1893, notes that the teller has plainly mixed two different accounts. In the third, the metropolitan Iliya, a man from al-Ahwaz, has a tomb built. For Hira he gives a tribute of 90,000 dirhams in one report and 190,000 in another.

The Jerusalem terms. Prym filled part of the text from two later writers, Mujir al-Din and al-Suyuti. He notes that M. J. de Goeje, who led the edition, had reason to think some words were not genuine. The terms as printed name no patriarch of Jerusalem.
His dates. Ginzel gives his life as the years 224 to 310 of the hijra and names no source. Hitti gives his death in 310 and places it in Baghdad. Neither gives a birthplace.
